feedback.note: The short formula and both halves of the longer clause are one statement, because the clause says what "applied to action" means: the nature determines the act, and the opposite act is out. A rival that suspends identity is not a third clause. Reading the halves as separate laws is how the formula gets cut off from its meaning.

exercises.prompt: Timber burns to ash, which fits what timber and fire are. Someone then demands that the same timber become marble because he prefers marble. Which demand does the full statement reject?

choices.text: The demand that the timber act as a different kind of entity
The burning, because any action violates the short formula
The ash, because change over time is a contradiction
Neither: preference is a minor cause the longer clause allows

feedback.note: Burning to ash is action that fits the entities, so the full statement accepts it, because identity applied to action is not a ban on action. Becoming marble by preference would be action against the timber's nature, which the longer clause rules out. The ash is change, not a contradiction. Preference is not a minor cause. The full statement draws that line and no other.

exercises.prompt: Complete the identity of the fuller statement.

parts.text: The fuller statement is still the law of

feedback.note: The fuller statement is still the law of identity, because the longer clause does not add a second ruler. Chance, decree, and conjunction are the rivals a "fuller" wording is sometimes asked to absorb. It does not absorb them. Spelling the law out, down to the ban on contradictory action, leaves it the same law.

exercises.prompt: Assemble the one-law claim in its fuller form.

feedback.note: Identity sets the action and bars its opposite, because that is the short formula and the longer clause in one line. "Chance" or "decree" would add a cause the law does not contain. The timber may burn; it may not become marble by a wish. A volitional consciousness, choosing to focus or not, is on the first side of that line: the action fits its nature.

exercises.prompt: What marks a fact as metaphysically given, rather than man-made?

choices.text: It is, it could not have been otherwise, and it must be accepted
It exists because someone chose to bring it about
It counts as given only when treating it as true is useful
It can be repealed when agreement runs the other way

feedback.note: A metaphysically given fact could not have been otherwise and must be accepted, because it is not a product of choice. Choice is what marks the man-made. Usefulness is the pragmatic test and does not decide what had to be. Agreement cannot repeal a natural fact. The given is accepted; it is not voted into being and not judged as if it might have failed to occur.

exercises.prompt: A mountain stands where the ground has raised it. No one decided to put it there. What kind of fact is it?

choices.text: A metaphysically given fact
A man-made fact, because people later named it
A wish, because travelers want a landmark
Not a fact, until a survey votes to recognize it

feedback.note: The mountain is metaphysically given, because no human choice brought it into existence and it could not have failed to be the formation it is. Naming it does not make it man-made. A traveler's wish is not the mountain. A survey apprehends it; the survey does not vote it into existence. Acceptance is the right response, not a ballot.

exercises.prompt: What does this passage establish about a natural event and about human action?
exercises.quote: Any natural phenomenon, i.e., any event which occurs without human participation, is the metaphysically given, and could not have occurred differently or failed to occur; any phenomenon involving human action is the man-made, and could have been different.

choices.text: A natural event could not have occurred differently; human action could have
A natural event is man-made whenever someone notices it
A natural event could have failed to occur if a vote had gone otherwise
Human action is metaphysically given in the same way as a natural event

feedback.quote: Any natural phenomenon, i.e., any event which occurs without human participation, is the metaphysically given, and could not have occurred differently or failed to occur; any phenomenon involving human action is the man-made, and could have been different.
feedback.citation: Ayn Rand, "The Metaphysical Versus the Man-Made," Philosophy: Who Needs It, 27
feedback.note: A natural phenomenon, an event without human participation, is metaphysically given and could not have occurred differently or failed to occur. A phenomenon involving human action is man-made and could have been different. Noticing does not turn the natural event into a choice. A vote cannot make it fail to have occurred. Human action is the other side of the distinction, not a second given.

exercises.prompt: Someone says a storm might have failed to occur, with no difference in the conditions, merely because it might have. What is the error?

choices.text: He treats a given event as if it could have been otherwise, which is the mark of the man-made
He has stated the definition of the metaphysically given
A possibility with no difference in conditions is what identity requires
The storm is man-made because people were soaked by it

feedback.note: A natural event could not have failed to occur given the conditions, because that necessity is what "metaphysically given" means. "Might have, with nothing different" is chance, and it borrows the modality of the man-made. Identity does not leave an event free of the entities that act. People getting wet does not make the storm a product of their choice.

exercises.prompt: Match each marker with the side of the distinction it belongs to.

pairs.left: Could not have failed to occur
pairs.right: The standing of a given fact
The response to a given fact
The standing of a man-made fact

feedback.note: A flood no one produced is given, it could not have failed to occur, and it must be accepted, because those three markers belong together. "Could have been different" marks the man-made, a product of choice. Swapping the markers would either demand a vote on the flood or demand uncritical acceptance of a choice. The two sides are not styles of speech about one kind of fact.

exercises.prompt: Someone says a given fact is "neither here nor there until we judge it true or false." What is the error?

choices.text: The given simply is; the true-or-false question belongs to one's judgment about it
Judgment creates the given fact
Acceptance is a vote, so the given waits on the tally
The given is false until it becomes useful

feedback.note: The metaphysically given cannot be true or false; it simply is, and a judgment is true or false by whether it matches the fact. Judging the fact itself as a candidate "until we decide" treats it as man-made. Judgment does not create it. Acceptance is not a vote. Usefulness is a pragmatic substitute for correspondence to the fact.

exercises.prompt: Complete the modality of a natural event.

parts.text: A natural phenomenon could not have occurred

feedback.note: A natural phenomenon could not have occurred differently, because no human choice was there to make a different outcome available. "By vote" and "by wish" name decrees the given does not admit. "Optionally" is the modality of the man-made, which could have been otherwise. The given must be accepted; it is not a menu.

exercises.prompt: Assemble the claim about the modality of the metaphysically given.

feedback.note: The given could not have been otherwise, because that is what separates it from a product of choice. "Voted" or "wished" would smuggle a human act into the modality of nature. The claim does not say a man-made fact could not have been otherwise. It says the opposite about that side. Acceptance, not judgment-as-if-optional, is the response.

exercises.prompt: What marks a fact as man-made, rather than metaphysically given?

choices.text: Choice brought it about, it did not have to be, and it must be judged
It could not have been otherwise, so it must be accepted uncritically
It is outside the power of any volition
It is not a fact at all, because a person produced it

feedback.note: A man-made fact is a product of choice: it did not have to be, and it must be judged, then kept or changed, because nothing made by man had to be. Uncritical acceptance is the response owed to the given, not to a choice. "Outside any volition" describes nature. Calling the product unreal denies that a bridge or a statute, once made, is a fact. It is a fact of a different kind.

exercises.prompt: A bridge stands because engineers designed it and crews built it. What kind of fact is the bridge?

choices.text: Man-made: it is a fact, and it did not have to exist
Metaphysically given, because it is now solid
Not a fact, because choice produced it
A wish, because someone wanted a crossing

feedback.note: The bridge is a man-made fact, because human choice brought it into existence and the choice could have gone another way. Solidity does not convert it into a mountain. It is still a fact; denying that confuses "did not have to be" with "is not." The wish to cross is not the bridge. The bridge must be judged, not accepted as nature.

exercises.prompt: What does this passage establish about things people make?
exercises.quote: Nothing made by man had to be: it was made by choice.

choices.text: Human products are facts that choice brought about, and they might not have been made
Human products are not facts
What man makes could not have been otherwise
A human product is the same kind of fact as a natural phenomenon

feedback.quote: Nothing made by man had to be: it was made by choice.
feedback.citation: Ayn Rand, "The Metaphysical Versus the Man-Made," Philosophy: Who Needs It, 27
feedback.note: Nothing made by man had to be, because it was made by choice. The product is still a fact; the passage does not say human works are unreal. "Could not have been otherwise" is the modality of the given, and a natural phenomenon is the other side of the distinction. The point is that the making was not necessary.

exercises.prompt: A cruel statute is on the books. Someone says, "It exists, so it must be accepted the way a flood is accepted." What is the error?

choices.text: Existence does not exempt a man-made fact from judgment; the statute can be rejected and changed
Every existent is metaphysically given
Judgment is a wish that the statute is not a fact
A statute is a natural phenomenon with no human part in it

feedback.note: The statute exists, and it is man-made, so it must be judged and may be changed, because nothing made by man had to be. Treating every existent as given erases the distinction. Judgment does not pretend the statute is unreal; it takes the fact and asks whether it should stand. A statute is human action, not a natural phenomenon.

exercises.prompt: Match each marker with the man-made side it names.

pairs.left: It did not have to be

pairs.right: The response a human product requires
The response a human product forbids

feedback.note: A code is man-made, it did not have to be, and it must be judged, because choice brought it about. Uncritical acceptance is owed to the given and forbidden here. Judging the code does not mean denying that it is on the books. The four markers keep the man-made side from collapsing into nature.

exercises.prompt: Someone says, "If we judge the statute, we are pretending it is not real." What is the answer?

choices.text: Judgment takes the statute as real and asks whether it should stand
Man-made facts are illusions, so the pretence is correct
Only wishes are real enough to judge
A fact that choice created is a contradiction and cannot be judged

feedback.note: Judgment presupposes the fact, because one judges what is, and then accepts or rejects and changes it when necessary. Man-made facts are not illusions. A wish is not the object of this judgment. A product of choice is not a contradiction; it is an entity or an arrangement human action brought about. Reality and "must be judged" are compatible.

exercises.prompt: Complete the reason a human product need not have existed.

parts.text: Nothing made by man had to be: it was made by

feedback.note: It was made by choice, because that is why a man-made fact could have been different. Nature and necessity are the modality of the given, and a flood is an instance of the given. None of those brought the statute or the bridge into existence. Choice did, and choice is what the judgment then evaluates.

exercises.prompt: Assemble the claim that a product of choice must be judged.

feedback.note: Choice made it, and it must be judged, because a man-made fact did not have to be and must not be accepted uncritically. "Accepted uncritically" is the response that belongs to the given. Using those words here would collapse the two sides. The fact remains a fact while it is judged. Judgment is not a wish that nothing was built.

exercises.prompt: What cannot settle a metaphysically given fact?

choices.text: A vote, a poll, or a majority
The nature of the entities involved
Observation of what actually occurred
Acceptance of what cannot be changed

feedback.note: A vote, a poll, or a majority cannot settle a given fact, because the given is outside the power of any volition and must be accepted. The natures of the entities are exactly what did settle it. Observation apprehends it. Acceptance is the right cognitive response, not a rival of the fact. The error is treating a tally as if it were a cause in nature.

exercises.prompt: A legislature votes that a flood did not happen. The water is in the houses. What does the vote accomplish?

choices.text: Nothing about the flood; a vote cannot rewrite a metaphysically given event
It makes the dryness a man-made fact in the houses
It must be accepted as the nature of the water
It makes the flood real only if the losing side perceived it

feedback.note: The vote cannot rewrite the flood, because a natural event could not have occurred differently and a tally is not one of its causes. The vote does not install dryness. The water's nature is not a statute. Perception does not decide whether the flood occurred. The legislature may judge its own relief statute. It may not vote the water away.

exercises.prompt: What does this passage establish about accepting facts of the two kinds?
exercises.quote: It is the metaphysically given that must be accepted: it cannot be changed. It is the man-made that must never be accepted uncritically: it must be judged, then accepted or rejected and changed when necessary.

choices.text: The given must be accepted because it cannot be changed; the man-made must be judged
Both kinds must be accepted uncritically
Both kinds are settled by vote
The given must be judged, and the man-made must be accepted as unchangeable

feedback.quote: It is the metaphysically given that must be accepted: it cannot be changed. It is the man-made that must never be accepted uncritically: it must be judged, then accepted or rejected and changed when necessary.
feedback.citation: Ayn Rand, "The Metaphysical Versus the Man-Made," Philosophy: Who Needs It, 27
feedback.note: The metaphysically given must be accepted, because it cannot be changed. The man-made must never be accepted uncritically: it must be judged, then accepted or rejected and changed when necessary. Treating both as uncritical, or both as votes, erases the distinction. Reversing the responses would put a flood up for a vote and a statute beyond repeal.

exercises.prompt: Someone says, "We cannot change the flood, so we also cannot change the relief statute." What is the answer?

choices.text: The flood is given; the statute is man-made and can be judged and changed
Both are outside the power of any volition
The relief statute is a natural phenomenon
Accepting the flood means accepting every policy adopted about it

feedback.note: The flood must be accepted because it cannot be changed. The statute must be judged because it was made by choice and could have been different. Putting both outside volition treats a law as a natural event. The statute is not a natural phenomenon. Policies about a flood are man-made even when the flood is not, so acceptance does not travel from one to the other.

exercises.prompt: Match each item with the response that fits it.

pairs.right: The response owed to the flood
The response open for the statute

feedback.note: The flood is given and must be accepted, because a vote cannot rewrite it. The statute is man-made and may be changed, because it did not have to be. "Must be accepted" does not transfer to the statute, and "may be changed" does not transfer to the water. The pair is the point of refusing to let a majority legislate nature.

exercises.prompt: A poll finds that most people feel a comet will miss the city. The orbit will not. What does the poll record?

choices.text: Feelings, which do not alter the given path
The orbit, which a majority feeling is competent to set
The metaphysically given, under the name of agreement
A man-made fact, because the poll mentioned the comet

feedback.note: The poll records feelings, and feelings do not rewrite a natural path, because the comet's course is metaphysically given. Subjective agreement is not the given. Mentioning the comet does not make the comet man-made. The error is the same one as the vote on the flood: a tally about a fact is not the fact.

exercises.prompt: Complete the limit on what a majority can rewrite.

feedback.note: A vote cannot rewrite a flood, because the flood is metaphysically given and could not have occurred differently. A statute can be rewritten by a later vote, which is why "statute" does not complete this limit. A wish or a feeling was never the kind of fact the vote was pretending to edit. The water remains the water.

exercises.prompt: Assemble the claim that a tally cannot edit the given.

feedback.note: A vote cannot change the metaphysically given, because the given must be accepted and cannot be changed. "Wish" would name a different non-cause, and "can" would reverse the limit. The claim does not say a vote cannot change a statute. A statute is man-made and is the thing a vote can change. The flood is not.

exercises.prompt: How does a wish stand to a metaphysically given fact?

choices.text: The wish is not the fact, and wanting the fact otherwise leaves the fact as it is
A strong wish is a second given fact that cancels the first
The wish turns the fact into a man-made fact
The fact is true or false according to the wish

feedback.note: A wish is not a fact, because wanting a given fact to be otherwise does not change it. A second, cancelling "given" made of desire is subjectivism. Wanting does not convert a natural event into a product of choice. The given cannot be true or false at all; truth belongs to the judgment that either matches the fact or contradicts it.

exercises.prompt: A farmer wants rain. The sky stays clear. What is the error in "my need is the sky"?

choices.text: The need is a wish; the clear sky is the given fact
The wish is metaphysically given and the sky is man-made
Wanting rain creates the rain, because consciousness apprehends needs
The sky is neither a fact nor the object of a wish

feedback.note: The clear sky is metaphysically given, and the need is a wish, so the need does not become the sky, because a wish is not a fact. Reversing which one is given inverts the distinction. Apprehension of a need is not creation of rain. The sky is a fact, and the wish is about it. They are not the same item under two names.

exercises.prompt: What does this passage establish about the given and about truth?
exercises.quote: The metaphysically given cannot be true or false, it simply is—and man determines the truth or falsehood of his judgments by whether they correspond to or contradict the facts of reality.

choices.text: The given simply is; a judgment is true or false by whether it matches the facts
The given is true when we wish it and false when we do not
Judgments have no truth; only wishes do
A fact that simply is can be voted false

feedback.quote: The metaphysically given cannot be true or false, it simply is—and man determines the truth or falsehood of his judgments by whether they correspond to or contradict the facts of reality.
feedback.citation: Ayn Rand, "The Metaphysical Versus the Man-Made," Philosophy: Who Needs It, 27
feedback.note: The metaphysically given cannot be true or false; it simply is. Man determines the truth or falsehood of his judgments by whether they correspond to or contradict the facts. A wish does not assign truth to the fact. Wishes are not the bearers of truth. A vote cannot make the given false. The error is moving truth from the judgment onto the fact, or onto the wish.

exercises.prompt: Someone says, "The drought is false because our judgment says there is rain." What is the right correction?

choices.text: The judgment that contradicts the drought is false; it does not make the drought false
The drought is true or false in itself, and the judgment's vote decides which
Correspondence means the fact must be brought into line with the wish
A drought is man-made whenever it is unwanted

feedback.note: The drought simply is, and the judgment that denies it is the thing that is false, because truth is correspondence to the facts, not a power to edit them. The given is not itself true or false. Correspondence does not run from wish to world. An unwanted drought is still a natural fact, not a product of the wanting. The wish remains a wish.

exercises.prompt: Match each item with what it is in the drought.

pairs.right: A given fact that simply is
Not a fact about the sky

pairs.left: A judgment that matches the drought
A judgment that denies the drought

feedback.note: The drought is given and simply is; the wish is not a fact about the sky, because wanting rain does not water the field. The matching judgment is true and the denying judgment is false by correspondence. Calling the wish a fact, or the drought false, swaps the given with a mental act. Truth stays on the side of the judgment.

exercises.prompt: A patient says, "I refuse the diagnosis, so the disease is not there." What does the refusal change?

choices.text: Nothing in the disease; the refusal is a wish about a given fact of the organism
The disease, which becomes man-made because a person is involved
The cells, whose nature is settled by the patient's vote
The diagnosis's words, and with them the cells, because words created the disease

feedback.note: The disease, as a condition of the organism occurring without being chosen, is metaphysically given, so the refusal does not erase it, because a wish is not a fact. A person's involvement does not make every bodily fact man-made; the choice would be a treatment, which is a different fact. A vote does not set the cells' nature. Words of a diagnosis identify or misidentify; they do not create the condition.

exercises.prompt: Complete the separation of wanting from what is.

feedback.note: A wish is not a fact, because the given simply is and wanting it otherwise leaves it as it is. "Feeling," "hope," and "fear" are the family of mental acts the wish already belongs to; they do not name what the wish fails to be. The word that completes the principle is fact. A judgment can report the fact. The wish cannot replace it.

exercises.prompt: Assemble the claim that wanting does not edit what is.

feedback.note: Wanting a fact otherwise does not change it, because a wish is not a fact and the given must be accepted. "Creates" or "erases" would give the wish the power of a decree. That is subjectivism, and it is the error the separation exists to block. The farmer's need and the patient's refusal are instances. The sky and the disease remain.

exercises.prompt: A river has cut a canyon, and a city has built a dam in it. How do you sort the two?

choices.text: The canyon's carving is given; the dam is man-made
Both are given, because both are there now
Both are man-made, because people live nearby
The canyon is a wish and the dam is a natural phenomenon

feedback.note: The carving is a natural phenomenon and could not have occurred differently; the dam was built by choice and did not have to be, because presence now does not put them in one class. Nearby people do not author the canyon. Reversing the labels treats a work of engineering as nature and a canyon as a wish. Each gets the response its side requires.

exercises.prompt: What does this passage establish about the mountain and the skyscraper?
exercises.quote: A skyscraper is a man-made fact, a mountain is a metaphysically given fact.

choices.text: Both are facts, and they are facts of different kinds
Both are metaphysically given once they exist
The skyscraper is given and the mountain is man-made
Neither is a fact until someone prefers it

feedback.quote: A skyscraper is a man-made fact, a mountain is a metaphysically given fact.
feedback.citation: Ayn Rand, "The Metaphysical Versus the Man-Made," Philosophy: Who Needs It, 31
feedback.note: A skyscraper is a man-made fact, and a mountain is a metaphysically given fact, so both are facts and the kind differs, because one was made by choice and the other was not. Existence does not collapse them into the given. Reversing them inverts the example. Preference does not decide which facts are real. The pair is the distinction in one line.

exercises.prompt: Someone says, "The mountain was not chosen, but a vote can classify it as a hill and be done." What can the vote do?

choices.text: It can adopt a policy or a name; it cannot make the mountain other than it is
It can change the given nature, because a classification is a cause
It can make the mountain man-made by naming it
It can leave acceptance of the mountain optional, in the way a statute is optional

feedback.note: A vote may set a legal label or a policy, which are man-made, but it cannot rewrite the mountain, because the mountain is given and could not have been otherwise. Classification is not a cause in the rock. Naming does not make a natural formation man-made. Acceptance of the mountain is not optional in the way a statute is. The statute, if any, is the thing to judge.

exercises.prompt: An engineer says the dam "had to be," in the same sense as the flood it blocks. What is the right split?

choices.text: The flood had to occur given the conditions; the dam did not have to be built
Both had to be, because both resist water
Neither had to be, because both involve water
The flood is man-made, because the dam was built in relation to it

feedback.note: The flood is a natural phenomenon and could not have failed to occur as it did; the dam was made by choice and might not have been built, because resisting water is not a shared modality. Water does not put every related fact on one side. Building a dam in relation to a flood does not reach backward and make the flood man-made. The engineer has used one phrase for two kinds of "had to."

exercises.prompt: Match each item with the kind of fact it is.

pairs.right: The mountain's standing as a natural fact

pairs.left: Must be judged, and may be changed
pairs.right: The response the skyscraper's existence allows

feedback.note: The mountain is given and could not have occurred differently; the skyscraper is man-made and must be judged, because the passage sets them on opposite sides while calling both facts. The response travels with the side. Accepting the skyscraper uncritically, or voting the mountain into a different nature, crosses the sides. Hold both at once.

exercises.prompt: A committee loves the mountain and hates the code that forbids building on its slope. What may the committee do?

choices.text: Accept the mountain, and judge the code, changing the code if the judgment requires it
Judge the mountain false, and accept the code uncritically because it is written
Treat both the mountain and the code as wishes
Treat both as outside the power of any volition

feedback.note: The mountain must be accepted, and the code must be judged, because one is given and the other is man-made. Reversing the responses, or calling both wishes, drops the distinction. The code is not outside volition; it was made by choice and can be changed. Love of the mountain is a feeling and does not add a second fact about the rock. Hatred of the code is not yet a judgment, but the code is the proper object of one.

exercises.prompt: Complete the contrast between a mountain and a skyscraper.

feedback.note: A mountain is metaphysically given, because it is not a product of choice, while a skyscraper is man-made. "Chosen," "voted," and "wished" are ways of producing or pretending to produce the man-made, and they do not describe the mountain. The line holds both sides only when the mountain stays on the given side. Both remain facts.

exercises.prompt: Assemble the two responses in their proper order.

feedback.note: Accept the given and judge the man-made, because the given cannot be changed and the man-made must not be accepted uncritically. "Rewrite" would aim the wrong response at nature, and "wish" would put a feeling in the place of either fact. The canyon and the mountain are accepted. The dam, the code, and the skyscraper are judged.

exercises.prompt: What is the primary act of volition, the choice the others depend on?

choices.text: The choice to focus the mind, or not to focus it
The choice of which percept the senses will deliver
The choice to make a given fact be otherwise
The choice of a conclusion reached with no effort to look

feedback.note: The primary choice is to focus or not, because to think or not is that choice, and it controls the choices that follow. Perception is not chosen; the sense organs do not pick what they deliver. A given fact is outside the power of volition. A conclusion with no effort to look is the refusal to focus, not a separate primary act that skips the choice.

exercises.prompt: A student lets the words slide, then tightens attention and works the argument. What was the choice?

choices.text: Whether to focus
Which sensations the eyes would deliver
The identity of the page
The truth of the theorem, settled by wanting it

feedback.note: Tightening attention is the choice to focus, and letting the words slide is the choice not to, because that alternative is the primary act of volition. The eyes deliver sensations without a vote. The page is what it is. Wanting does not settle the theorem. Later choices about what to say come after this one and depend on it.

exercises.prompt: What does this passage establish about the choice to think or not?
exercises.quote: Psychologically, the choice "to think or not" is the choice "to focus or not."

choices.text: The choice to think or not is the choice to focus or not
Thinking is a percept, and focus is a later optional extra
To think or not means to pick which sensations arrive
Focus is compelled, and choice begins only after a proof is finished

feedback.quote: Psychologically, the choice "to think or not" is the choice "to focus or not."
feedback.citation: Ayn Rand, "The Objectivist Ethics," The Virtue of Selfishness, 21
feedback.note: The passage identifies the choice to think or not with the choice to focus or not, so the primary act is that effort, not a selection among percepts. Thinking is not a percept. Sensations are not chosen. Focus is not compelled, and it is not postponed until a finished proof, because the proof is work the focus makes possible. The line names one choice.

exercises.prompt: Someone says, "I will decide what is true after I have already refused to look." Where is the volition in that plan?

choices.text: The refusal to look is already the choice not to focus
Not looking is a percept he chose to have
The later decision is primary, and the drift is metaphysically given
Focus would be the same act as agreeing with a crowd

feedback.note: Refusing to look is the choice not to focus, because there is no neutral gap before volition in which one simply has not chosen. Not looking is not a selected percept. Drift is not a metaphysically given fact about the page; the page is given, and the drift is an act of the mind. Agreement with a crowd is a later, different choice, and it is not what focus means.

exercises.prompt: Match each item with its relation to the primary choice.

pairs.left: A later decision about what to say
pairs.right: A choice that focus makes possible
Not a power of this choice

feedback.note: Focus or not is primary, a percept is not chosen, and later decisions depend on the focus, because the choice to think is the choice to focus. Deciding does not rewrite a given fact. Treating a percept as chosen, or a decree as thinking, moves volition to the wrong level. The primary act is the effort, not the content and not a vote over nature.

exercises.prompt: Someone says free will is the power to make the page say whatever he wants. What has he confused?

choices.text: The choice to think with a decree over the given
Nothing: making the page obey is the primary choice
The page's identity, which attention is free to assign
Focus, which creates the text it attends to

feedback.note: Free will is the freedom to think or not, not a power to make the page be otherwise, because the given is outside any volition. Attention does not assign the page's identity. Focus does not create the text; it apprehends it, or it fails to. The confusion is primacy of consciousness wearing the name of volition. The choice is real, and its object is the mind's effort.

exercises.prompt: Complete the name of the primary choice.

feedback.note: The primary choice is to focus or not, because that is the choice to think or not. Perceiving is not chosen. Voting and wishing are not the primary act, and neither rewrites the given. Later choices about content presuppose this one. The act named is the effort, not a percept and not a decree.

exercises.prompt: Assemble the statement of the primary choice.

feedback.note: The primary choice is to focus or not, because every later choice depends on whether the mind exerts that effort. "Perceive" would move volition to the senses, which have no such choice. "Decree" would move it over the facts. The primary act does not select sensations and does not edit nature. It is the choice to think or not.

exercises.prompt: Which line correctly separates what is chosen from what is not?

choices.text: Focus is chosen; perception is not
Percepts are chosen, and focus is automatic
Both percepts and the given facts are chosen
Neither focus nor a later inference is chosen

feedback.note: Focus is volitional and perception is not, because the pre-conceptual level is nonvolitional and the choice to think is the choice to focus. Chosen percepts reverse that order. The given facts are not chosen either, but that is a further point; the error in the third option is already the claim that percepts are chosen. Inference is work the focus makes possible, so it is not outside volition.

exercises.prompt: You walk into a bright room. The glare is there before you decide anything. What is the glare?

choices.text: A percept, delivered without a choice
A syllogism
The primary choice
A man-made fact you enacted by entering

feedback.note: The glare is a percept, and the perceptual level is nonvolitional, because the sense organs do not choose or invent what they deliver. It is not a syllogism, which belongs to the conceptual level where volition operates. It is not the choice to focus. Entering the room may have been chosen; the glare, once the eyes are open, was not enacted as a man-made fact.

exercises.prompt: What does this passage establish about where volition begins?
exercises.quote: The pre-conceptual level of consciousness is nonvolitional; volition begins with the first syllogism.

choices.text: Volition begins at the conceptual level; percepts are not chosen
Percepts are chosen, and the first syllogism is what a percept is
A finished syllogism comes before any choice to focus, so focus is compelled
Volition begins by rewriting the deliveries of perception

feedback.quote: The pre-conceptual level of consciousness is nonvolitional; volition begins with the first syllogism.
feedback.citation: Ayn Rand, "For the New Intellectual," For the New Intellectual, 14
feedback.note: The pre-conceptual level is nonvolitional, and volition begins with the first syllogism, so the line marks the conceptual level rather than a power to choose percepts. It does not say a finished inference precedes the choice to focus. Focus is the primary choice at that level, the choice that makes concept-formation and inference possible. The line does not rewrite what perception gave.

exercises.prompt: How does "volition begins with the first syllogism" sit with "to think or not is to focus or not"?

choices.text: Both locate one choice at the conceptual level: focus, which makes thinking possible
They contradict, so one of the two lines has to be dropped
The syllogism line means percepts are chosen, and the focus line denies every choice
Focus is pre-conceptual, and the syllogism is a natural event like a flood

feedback.note: The syllogism marks the conceptual level, and at that level the primary choice is to focus or not, because concept-formation and inference are the work focus makes possible. The lines do not contradict. They do not mean percepts are chosen, and they do not cancel the choice. Focus is not a percept, and a syllogism is not a flood. Reading them as a clash flattens two statements of one fact.

exercises.prompt: Match each mental item with the volitional status it has.

pairs.right: Conceptual work, not a chosen percept

feedback.note: Perception is nonvolitional, focus is the primary choice, and concept-formation and inference are what that choice makes possible, because volition begins at the conceptual level. An inference is not a percept one selected. Calling the concept a chosen sensation, or the percept a syllogism, swaps the levels the two lines exist to separate.

exercises.prompt: "Volition begins with the first syllogism" is read as "you choose the sensation, and logic then runs by itself." What has the reading reversed?

choices.text: The pre-conceptual level is the nonvolitional one, and choice operates at the conceptual level
Nothing: that reading is what nonvolitional means
Sensations, which are man-made facts
A syllogism, which is a metaphysically given flood of sound

feedback.note: The reading reverses the line, because the pre-conceptual level, including percepts, is nonvolitional, and the syllogism names where volition begins. "Nonvolitional" does not mean the sensation was chosen. Sensations are not man-made facts. A syllogism is conceptual work, not a natural flood. The primary choice inside that work is still to focus or not, which is what makes the inference possible.

exercises.prompt: Complete the volitional status of perception.

feedback.note: Perception is not chosen, because the pre-conceptual level is nonvolitional and the organs do not elect their deliveries. Perception is real, it is a form of the given in awareness, and it is caused by the entities perceived and by the nature of the sense organs. Those words do not complete the volitional point. The word that does is chosen, and the answer is that it is not.

exercises.prompt: Assemble what the choice to focus makes possible.

feedback.note: Focus makes concept-formation and inference possible, because those are the conceptual activities volition begins, and percepts are not among the things it chooses. "Percepts chosen" would reverse the levels. The first syllogism is not a rival of focus and not a step that happens before any choice to think. It is the mark of the level at which that choice operates.

exercises.prompt: Why is the choice to think or not classified as axiomatic?

choices.text: An attempt to deny the choice already uses the choice to think
A vote has defined free will into existence
Volition is proved from a standpoint outside consciousness
Determinism is true, so the claim of choice is an optional hypothesis

feedback.note: Volition is axiomatic because any attempt to deny the choice to think must use that choice: the denial is an act of focusing. A vote does not make an axiom. There is no standpoint outside consciousness from which one could show that no one is conscious of choosing. Determinism, read as "there is no alternative of focus," is the claim the denial is trying to establish, and the denial enacts the alternative.

exercises.prompt: A speaker argues, carefully and at length, that no one chooses to think. What is he doing in the arguing?

choices.text: He is focusing in order to deny focus, so the denial uses the choice
He is reporting a percept that he chose to have
He has stepped outside consciousness and observed that choice is absent
He has shown that thinking is a natural event of the same kind as a flood

feedback.note: The argument is an act of focus directed at a conclusion, so it uses the choice it denies, because that is the axiomatic pattern. He did not choose the percepts that came while he worked; he chose to think. There is no outside of consciousness for the inspection. Thinking is not a flood. A flood could not have been otherwise and involves no choice to focus. His article did.

exercises.prompt: What does this passage establish about free will?
exercises.quote: That which you call your soul or spirit is your consciousness, and that which you call "free will" is your mind's freedom to think or not, the only will you have, your only freedom, the choice that controls all the choices you make and determines your life and your character.

choices.text: Free will is the mind's freedom to think or not, the choice that controls the others
Free will is the power to make given facts be otherwise
The soul is a thing apart from consciousness
Character is innate, and the choice to think does not shape it

feedback.quote: That which you call your soul or spirit is your consciousness, and that which you call "free will" is your mind's freedom to think or not, the only will you have, your only freedom, the choice that controls all the choices you make and determines your life and your character.
feedback.citation: Ayn Rand, Galt's Speech, For the New Intellectual, 127
feedback.note: The passage says the soul or spirit is one's consciousness, and free will is the mind's freedom to think or not, the choice that controls the others, because that is the only will one has. It does not name a power over the given. The soul is not a second thing beside consciousness. Character follows this choice rather than replacing it as an innate given.

exercises.prompt: Someone says, "If every choice has a cause, there is no volition." What is the answer?

choices.text: The cause is the nature of a volitional consciousness, which includes the alternative of focus
A cause means a divine decree, so volition would require one
Volition has to be chance, or else it is not real
Axioms apply only to bodies, so the mind is exempt from causality

feedback.note: The choice to focus or not is the action of a volitional consciousness according to its nature, so a cause does not erase it, because causality is identity applied to action. A decree is the wrong kind of cause. Chance would make the choice a break in causality rather than an instance of it. Minds are not exempt from identity. Determinism, in the form "no alternative is open," denies the nature rather than applying it.

exercises.prompt: Match each item with what it is in the account of free will.

pairs.left: A push with no alternative of focus
A wish that rewrites the given

feedback.note: Free will is the freedom to think or not, and a denial that uses thought fails because it enacts the axiom. Determinism here means a push that leaves no alternative of focus, which denies the nature of this consciousness. A wish that rewrites the given is a decree, not the will the passage names. The only will one has is the choice that controls the other choices.

exercises.prompt: Someone says people simply are rational or not, the way a stone falls, so there is no choice to focus. What is the right contrast?

choices.text: A stone cannot choose; a volitional consciousness can, and that difference is its nature
Men and stones have the same kind of action
Focus is a percept, so the contrast never arises
Rationality is a majority vote about who counts as a thinker

feedback.note: A stone acts as a stone and has no alternative of focus; a person is a being of volitional consciousness, so the choice to focus or not is his nature in action, because the difference is identity, not an exemption from causality. The actions are not the same kind. Focus is not a percept. A vote does not assign rationality. Denying the difference treats a mind as a stone and then uses a mind to say so.

exercises.prompt: Complete the reason a denial of the choice fails.

parts.text: To deny the choice to think, a speaker must

feedback.note: The speaker must use the choice, because the denial is an act of thinking and an axiom is what one uses in the attempt to deny it. Escape is what the axiom rules out. Perception is not the act he is performing when he argues, and a vote does not validate or cancel an axiom. The failure is internal to the argument.

exercises.prompt: Assemble the reason the denial of volition fails.

feedback.note: Denying the choice to think already uses it, because the denier is focusing in order to argue. "Escapes" would claim the exit the axiom closes. "Perception" would put the act at the pre-conceptual level, which is not where this choice sits. The freedom to think or not is the only will one has, and it is in use in the very sentence that calls it a myth.

exercises.prompt: How does volition stand to the metaphysically given?

choices.text: The given is not chosen; choice can add man-made facts and cannot rewrite the given
Volition's work is to vote the given out of existence
The given is whatever focus creates
Man-made facts are outside choice, and the given is inside it

feedback.note: The given is not chosen, and the nature of nature is outside the power of any volition, because choice can bring man-made facts into existence and cannot make a natural fact be otherwise. Voting the given away is the decree this limit rejects. Focus does not create the given. Reversing the two sides puts choice where acceptance belongs and acceptance where judgment belongs.

exercises.prompt: You choose to build a levee. You do not choose the flood's depth. What is the split?

choices.text: The flood is given; the levee is a man-made fact the choice can bring about
Both are chosen, because you are present
The levee is given and the flood is a syllogism
Focus makes the flood's depth whatever the plan requires

feedback.note: The flood's depth is a natural fact and could not have been otherwise; the levee is man-made and did not have to be, because your presence does not choose the water. The levee is not given, and the flood is not an inference. Focus can identify the depth and can direct the building. It cannot set the depth to match the plan. That would be a decree over the given.

exercises.prompt: What does this passage establish about volition and nature?
exercises.quote: Nature is the metaphysically given—i.e., the nature of nature is outside the power of any volition.

choices.text: No choice, including the choice to focus, can rewrite the nature of nature
Volition creates nature
The given is outside volition only until the first syllogism
Man-made facts are outside volition in the same way nature is

feedback.quote: Nature is the metaphysically given—i.e., the nature of nature is outside the power of any volition.
feedback.citation: Ayn Rand, "The Metaphysical Versus the Man-Made," Philosophy: Who Needs It, 25
feedback.note: Nature is the metaphysically given, and the nature of nature is outside the power of any volition, so focus cannot rewrite it. Volition does not create nature. The first syllogism marks where choice begins in the mind; it does not annex nature. Man-made facts are the opposite case: they are inside the power of choice and must be judged. The passage draws the line on nature's side.

exercises.prompt: Someone says, "I focused, so the percepts, which I did not choose, became optional." What is the error?

choices.text: Focus does not reach back and make perception a choice, and it does not make the given optional
The first syllogism chooses the sensations it rests on
A percept is man-made because thinking follows it
Outside the power of volition means outside existence

feedback.note: Focus operates at the conceptual level and leaves percepts nonvolitional, because the pre-conceptual level is not chosen and the given is not optional. A syllogism does not elect its sensory basis. A percept is not man-made merely because one thinks about it. "Outside volition" does not mean outside existence; the given exists, and that is why it must be accepted rather than edited.

exercises.prompt: Match each item in the levee case with its status.

pairs.left: The decision to raise a levee

feedback.note: The depth and the nature of water are given and not chosen, the decision is the choice, and the levee is the man-made fact that choice can add, because volition comes after the given and does not replace it. Swapping the levee onto the given side, or the flood onto the chosen side, is the collapse this order exists to prevent.

exercises.prompt: A council says, "We focused honestly, therefore the comet's orbit ought to match our plan." What did the honest focus do?

choices.text: It identified the orbit, or it failed to; it did not put the orbit under their choice
It decreed the orbit
It made the orbit man-made, because they thought about it
It made the plan metaphysically given, because the plan was sincere

feedback.note: Honest focus is the choice to think, and thinking apprehends the orbit, because the orbit is given and outside the power of volition. Focus is not a decree. Thinking about a natural fact does not make it man-made. Sincerity does not make a plan into nature. The plan is man-made and must be judged against the orbit, which must be accepted.

exercises.prompt: Complete the limit on what choice can reach.

parts.text: The nature of nature is outside the power of any

feedback.note: The nature of nature is outside the power of any volition, because the given is not chosen. Perception apprehends it and does not author it. Identity is what the nature is, not a power over it. A flood is an instance of the given, not the name of the limit. The limit is volition: choice can add a levee and cannot choose the water.

exercises.prompt: Assemble the boundary between choice and the given.

feedback.note: Choice adds the man-made and leaves the given, because volition stands after the metaphysically given and cannot rewrite the nature of nature. "Rewrites nature" is the decree the boundary rejects. The levee is the addition. The flood's depth and the comet's orbit stay where they are. Focus is a choice inside that boundary, not a tool for crossing it.

exercises.prompt: Which order states the relation of the given, the choice, and the axiom?

choices.text: The given first, then the choice to focus or not, and that choice is axiomatic
The choice first, which creates the given, with the axiom supplied by a vote
Percepts chosen first, then a syllogism that rewrites them, then a decree
Man-made facts accepted uncritically, then a flood chosen by focus

feedback.note: The given comes first and is not chosen; the primary choice is to focus or not; and that choice is axiomatic because a denial of it uses it. Choice does not create the given, and a vote does not make the axiom. Percepts are not chosen, and a syllogism does not rewrite them. Man-made facts are judged, and a flood is not chosen. The order is given, then the choice, then the axiomatic standing of that choice.

exercises.prompt: A critic argues that there is no choice to think. A storm, during the argument, is not under his will. What does the case contain?

choices.text: A given he cannot rewrite, a focus his argument uses, and an axiom the denial enacts
A storm he chose and an argument that was only a percept
Proof that volition starts by editing the storm
Proof that the first syllogism is a natural event of the same kind as the storm

feedback.note: The storm is given and outside volition; the argument is an act of focus; the denial uses the choice and so confirms the axiom, because those are the three points in one case. He did not choose the storm, and the argument is not a percept. Volition does not edit the storm. A syllogism is conceptual and chosen in the sense that focus makes it possible; it is not a flood. The case holds the order together.

exercises.prompt: What does this passage establish about the act of focusing?
exercises.quote: The act of focusing one's consciousness is volitional.

choices.text: The act of focusing is a matter of choice
The act of focusing is compelled, with no alternative open
The act of focusing creates the objects that are perceived
The act of focusing is a pre-conceptual percept

feedback.quote: The act of focusing one's consciousness is volitional.
feedback.citation: Ayn Rand, "The Objectivist Ethics," The Virtue of Selfishness, 21
feedback.note: The passage says the act of focusing one's consciousness is volitional, so the act is chosen. It does not say the act is compelled, which would be determinism of the "no alternative" kind. It does not say focus creates its objects. Focus is not a percept; perception is the nonvolitional level. The sentence names the primary choice and leaves the given unedited.

exercises.prompt: Where does "volition begins with the first syllogism" fit this order?

choices.text: It places the start of volition at the conceptual level, after a given that was not chosen
It places volition before the given, as the author of nature
It makes the first percept into a syllogism
It means there is no choice until a logic course has been completed

feedback.note: The line places volition at the conceptual level, where the primary choice is to focus, and it leaves the given and the percepts unchosen, because "first syllogism" names that level rather than a finished proof that precedes effort. It does not author nature. It does not turn a percept into an inference. A logic course is one man-made occasion for thinking, not the start of the capacity. The order stays: given, then the choice.

exercises.prompt: Match each item with its place in the order.

pairs.left: What could not have been otherwise
A denial that uses the choice

pairs.right: A man-made fact added by choice

feedback.note: The given could not have been otherwise, focus or not is the primary choice, a denial that uses the choice shows the axiom, and a levee is the man-made fact choice can add, because that is the order. The levee is not given, the flood is not axiomatic volition, and the denial is not a percept. Holding the four apart is the integration.

exercises.prompt: Someone says, "If volition is axiomatic, it is a given, so the choice to focus could not have been otherwise." What has he collapsed?

choices.text: He has collapsed the choice into the given; focus could have gone the other way
Nothing: axiomatic means metaphysically forced
Nothing: "could have been otherwise" applies only to floods, never to choices
The first syllogism, which he correctly treats as compelled

feedback.note: Axiomatic does not mean "could not have been otherwise." The given is what could not have been otherwise; the choice to focus could have been the choice not to focus, because that alternative is the nature of a volitional consciousness. "Could have been otherwise" also marks man-made facts, not only floods. The syllogism is not compelled. The collapse erases the difference the order exists to keep.

exercises.prompt: Complete the point that keeps the choice from being a given fact.

parts.text: The choice to focus could have gone the

feedback.note: The choice could have gone the other way, because focus or not is an alternative, not a natural event that had to occur. "Only," "given," and "forced" would collapse the choice into the metaphysically given or into determinism. The axiom says you use the choice when you deny it. It does not say you had no alternative. The storm had no alternative. The argument did.

exercises.prompt: Assemble the order of the given and the choice.

feedback.note: The given is first, and focus is axiomatic, because nature is outside volition and the choice to focus is what a denial must use. "Creates" would let focus author the given. "Percepts" would put the axiom at the wrong level, since percepts are not chosen. The order does not make the choice unchangeable in the way a flood is unchangeable. It makes the choice undeniable without being used.

exercises.prompt: What contrast does existence draw, once "something" is taken seriously?

choices.text: To be something, as against the nothing of nonexistence
To be a floating attribute with no thing that has it
To be whatever a mind produces
To be nothing in particular, and still to exist

feedback.note: To exist is to be something, as distinguished from the nothing of nonexistence, because a nothing does not exist. A floating attribute has no entity. A mind's product would make the something depend on consciousness. "Nothing in particular" is a something with the nature erased, which is not a third kind of being. The contrast is something against nothing.

exercises.prompt: Someone says, "There is a nothing out there, and it is a kind of thing." What is the error?

choices.text: Nonexistence is not a something; to exist is already to be something
Nothing is an entity, and it has the attribute of vacancy
A void of that kind is a man-made fact
To be is to be perceived, so an unseen nothing is an entity

feedback.note: A nothing that is a kind of thing has been turned into a something, which contradicts the contrast, because nonexistence is not an entity with attributes. Vacancy as an attribute still needs an entity that has it. A void is not man-made by being called a thing. "To be is to be perceived" does not rescue an unseen nothing; it is a different error, about existence depending on a mind.

exercises.prompt: What does this passage establish about whatever exists?
exercises.quote: To exist is to be something, as distinguished from the nothing of nonexistence, it is to be an entity of a specific nature made of specific attributes.

choices.text: What exists is an entity of a specific nature, made of specific attributes
What exists may be an attribute with no entity
Nonexistence is a place stocked with vague somethings
Nature and attributes are optional extras on a bare existence

feedback.quote: To exist is to be something, as distinguished from the nothing of nonexistence, it is to be an entity of a specific nature made of specific attributes.
feedback.citation: Ayn Rand, Galt's Speech, For the New Intellectual, 124
feedback.note: To exist is to be something, as against the nothing of nonexistence: an entity of a specific nature made of specific attributes. An attribute with no entity is not that something. Nonexistence is not a place. Nature and attributes are not extras, because without them there is no something to point to. The passage states the whole requirement in one sentence.

exercises.prompt: Someone grants that something exists, then adds that it has no nature yet. What has he granted and then withdrawn?

choices.text: A something with no nature would not be distinguishable from nothing
Nothing: identity is assigned later by consciousness, and existence can wait
Nothing: nature is man-made, and existence is not
Nothing: attributes come first, and the entity is a later vote

feedback.note: He has withdrawn the something, because to exist is to be something of a specific nature, and a nature-free item is not distinct from nonexistence. Consciousness does not assign identity later; it identifies the nature that is already there. Nature is not man-made. Attributes are not prior votes that compose an entity after the fact. They are how the specific nature is constituted.

exercises.prompt: Match each expression with what it names.

feedback.note: Something is what exists, nothing is what does not, and the something must have a specific nature, because those are the terms of the contrast. A feature with no entity is not a something and not a respectable nothing; it is a confusion of an attribute with an existent. Existence is not a bare act added to either.

exercises.prompt: Someone speaks of "existence in general," a being with no entity and no attributes. What is that expression naming?

choices.text: Nothing one can point to; what exists is some specific entity
The first entity, of which specific things are later cuts
A formless given, which minds cut into man-made things
Kant's forms, which are the something

feedback.note: There is no existence-in-general, because to exist is to be an entity of a specific nature made of specific attributes. Specific things are not cuts in a formless being. Calling that being a given, and the entities man-made, reverses the metaphysical order. Kant's forms are a claim about the mind's structuring, not a something that replaces entities. The expression names no existent.

exercises.prompt: Complete the contrast with nonexistence.

parts.text: , as against the nothing of nonexistence.

feedback.note: To exist is to be something, because the nothing of nonexistence is the contrasted term, not a rival kind of being. "Nothing" would collapse the contrast. A wish is not an existent. An attribute is not, by itself, the something; it is an attribute of an entity. What exists is something, and the something is an entity.

exercises.prompt: Assemble the contrast between existing and not existing.

feedback.note: To exist is to be something, not nothing, because that is the contrast the axiom draws. "A wish" would put a mental act in the place of the something. The claim does not say an attribute can stand in for the entity. The something is an entity of a specific nature, made of specific attributes, and nonexistence supplies no such entity.

exercises.prompt: What, in this account, is an entity, as against a loose feature?

choices.text: A something with a specific nature and specific attributes
A feature floating free of any thing
A word that need not refer to anything
An action with no actor

feedback.note: An entity is a something with a specific nature and specific attributes, because to exist is to be that, and not a loose feature, an empty word, or an action with nothing acting. Attributes do not float free of an entity. An action follows from what the entity is. Dropping the entity leaves a word or a feature with nothing to belong to.

exercises.prompt: People discuss "redness" as if it traveled on its own, with no apple, cloth, or light. What is missing?

choices.text: The entity that has the attribute
A vote declaring that redness exists alone
A decree that creates redness without a thing
A constant conjunction between two nothings

feedback.note: Redness is an attribute of some entity, so the apple or the cloth is what is missing, because attributes do not float free. A vote or a decree would try to install a free-floating feature by consciousness, which is primacy of consciousness applied to metaphysics. Constant conjunction of nothings is not an entity either. The attribute has to be the attribute of something.

exercises.prompt: Which of these is an entity, rather than something said about an entity?

choices.text: A particular tree
The green of the tree, offered as a separate existent
The tree's growth, offered with no tree
The thesis that only ideas exist

feedback.note: The tree is an entity, because it is a something of a specific nature. The green is an attribute of the tree, and the growth is an action of the tree; neither exists as a separate thing once the tree is dropped. "Only ideas exist" is idealism, not an example of an entity. The question is which item is the something, and the something is the tree.

exercises.prompt: Someone says an entity is only a bundle of loose attributes, and the bundle is nothing over and above those loose items. What has he dropped?

choices.text: The entity: the attributes are its attributes, not a crowd that replaces it
Nothing: a crowd of attributes is the primacy of existence
Nothing: attributes are man-made and the entity is a wish
Nothing: identity allows the attributes to contradict one another at the same time

feedback.note: He has dropped the entity, because attributes do not float free and a crowd of them is not a substitute for the something that has them. That picture is not the primacy of existence. Attributes are not man-made additions to a wish. Identity does not allow contradictory attributes in the same respect at the same time. The bundle language is a way of saying there is no entity.

exercises.prompt: Match each item with its metaphysical role.

feedback.note: The tree is the entity, green is one of its attributes, and growing is one of its actions, because an attribute and an action belong to the something and do not replace it. Green with no tree is the floating-attribute error. Treating the action as the entity, or the color as a second tree, loses the something whose nature those items express.

exercises.prompt: Someone says, "The motion exists, and the ball is our optional picture of it." What is the right order?

choices.text: The motion is the ball's action; without the ball there is no motion
Actions are the entities, and balls are their attributes
A ball is man-made and motion is a given nothing
Perception creates the ball around a free-floating motion

feedback.note: The ball is the entity and the motion is its action, because action follows from what the entity is and does not precede it as a free-floating fact. Reversing entity and attribute drops the something. The ball is not man-made by being round, and motion is not a nothing. Perception apprehends the ball; it does not build one around an orphaned motion.

exercises.prompt: Complete the dependence of an attribute on what has it.

parts.text: An attribute does not float free of an

feedback.note: An attribute does not float free of an entity, because the attribute is a way that something is, not a something of its own. A wish, a vote, or a void does not supply the missing bearer. The void is nonexistence, not an entity that could have attributes. The principle keeps redness, motion, and green attached to the things that have them.

exercises.prompt: Assemble the definition of an entity as a something.

feedback.note: An entity is a something with specific attributes, because that is what it is to be something rather than a loose feature. "Floating" and "wishes" are the errors: an attribute cut off from the entity, or a mental act in its place. The definition also includes a specific nature, which those attributes constitute. A word, by itself, is not the entity.

exercises.prompt: What kind of nature does an entity have?

choices.text: A specific nature, not an open character that could be anything
No nature, until a mind assigns one
Every incompatible nature at once, in the same respect
A nature that forbids the entity to act

feedback.note: An entity has a specific nature, because to exist is to be something in particular, not an open character. A mind does not assign the nature. Incompatible natures at once would be a contradiction, which is an error in thinking. Specificity does not forbid action; it limits action to what that nature does. Openness would be a something that is also nothing in particular.

exercises.prompt: Can this piece of metal be, in the same respect and at the same time, a perfect insulator and a perfect conductor?

choices.text: No: that would be both what it is and not what it is
Yes: a specific nature means an open character
Yes, if a vote declares both
Yes: change over time allows both at the same time

feedback.note: It cannot be both in the same respect at the same time, because that is a contradiction and a specific nature excludes it. An open character is the error the principle rejects. A vote cannot rewrite the metal. Change over time is a different state later, not both states at once. The metal is what it is, and the incompatible pair is an error in the description.

exercises.prompt: This metal conducts. A different alloy, prepared later, insulates. What is that difference?

choices.text: Two natures, or two states, across time; not one contradiction
Proof that a specific nature forbids any later difference
The later alloy rewriting the earlier metal's past
Conductivity as a wish rather than an attribute

feedback.note: A later alloy is a different entity, or a changed state at a different time, so there is no contradiction, because identity rules out both at once in the same respect, not change. Specific nature does not freeze every later difference. The later fact does not rewrite the earlier one. Conductivity is an attribute of the metal that has it, not a wish about metal in general.

exercises.prompt: Someone says, "If the entity has a specific nature, it cannot melt, burn, or move." What is the inference's error?

choices.text: Those actions can be what that nature does; specificity is not stillness
A specific nature means the entity is only a word
Motion is the primacy of consciousness
Melting is man-made, so the ban is right for natural entities

feedback.note: Melting, burning, and moving can be actions that follow from what the entity is, because A is A does not mean a thing cannot act. Specific nature is not a word in place of a thing. Motion is not a mental product. Melting of a natural substance is not man-made. The inference confuses "it is this, and not the opposite" with "it does nothing."

exercises.prompt: Match each expression with what it means for a nature.

pairs.right: The error of saying it could be anything

pairs.left: The same respect at the same time
pairs.right: Where a contradiction would have to be claimed
Change, which is not a contradiction

feedback.note: A specific nature is what the entity is, and an open character denies that, because a thing cannot be anything and still be something. A contradiction is a clash in the same respect at the same time. A later state is change. Mixing the last two either freezes the entity or pretends it is both of two opposites now.

exercises.prompt: Someone says that, under the mind's forms, the metal has no nature as it is, only a nature for us. What has he done with the nature?

choices.text: He has given it to the mind's structuring and dropped the entity's own identity
He has stated what a specific nature means
He has reported Kant's claim that wishes are metals
He has classified the metal as a man-made structure

feedback.note: A nature "for us," with none as the metal is, is Kant's claim that the mind's forms structure what we can know, so we do not know the thing as it is, and that is primacy of consciousness, because the identity has been moved into the mind. It is not the definition of a specific nature. It is not the caricature that wishes are metals. The metal is not man-made by being known.

exercises.prompt: Complete the kind of nature an entity has.

feedback.note: The nature is specific, because an open, optional, voted, or dual character would let the entity be and not be in the same respect. "Dual" is the contradiction, not a richer nature. "Voted" and "optional" hand the nature to consciousness. Specificity still allows action and change. It does not allow the metal to be both conductor and insulator at once.

exercises.prompt: Assemble the rejection of an open character.

feedback.note: A specific nature is not an open character, because to be something is to be something in particular. A wish or a vote would make the nature depend on consciousness, which is a different error and not the claim. The metal remains a conductor or it does not, in the respect at issue. Later change is still available. Both-at-once is not.

exercises.prompt: How do attributes stand to the entity that has them?

choices.text: They make up its nature, and they belong to it
They exist loose, and the entity is a label added later
They are created by the act of noticing them
They may contradict one another in the same respect and still be its nature

feedback.note: Attributes are the specific characteristics that make up the entity's nature, and they belong to the entity, because a nature is not a label on a pile of free items. Noticing identifies attributes; it does not create them. A contradiction among them, in the same respect at once, is an error in thinking, not a richer nature. The attributes are how the something is specific.

exercises.prompt: A pane of glass is transparent, brittle, and solid. What are those three?

choices.text: Specific attributes of the glass
Entities that could remain if the glass were gone and only they were kept
Man-made facts, because someone listed them
Forms of intuition, with no glass required

feedback.note: They are attributes of the glass, because they are ways that entity is, and they do not survive as existents if one pretends the glass is gone. Listing them does not make them man-made. Calling them forms of intuition, with no glass, is Kant's move: the mind's structuring in place of the thing. The pane is the entity. Transparency, brittleness, and solidity are its attributes.

exercises.prompt: Someone says, "Take away every attribute and the entity remains, as a bare particular." What remains, on this account?

choices.text: Nothing one can call a specific something
The entity, correctly, since attributes are decorations
The metaphysically given, with the attributes as later votes
A clear case of action following from a nature

feedback.note: A bare particular with no attributes is not a specific something, because an entity is of a specific nature made of specific attributes. Attributes are not decorations. They are not votes added to a given blank. Action follows from a nature that has attributes, so the bare item supplies nothing for an action to follow from. Removing the attributes removes the entity.

exercises.prompt: Match each item in the glass example with what it is.

pairs.left: Fully brittle and fully elastic in one blow, same respect
pairs.right: Not a real pair of attributes

feedback.note: The pane is the entity and transparency is its attribute, because the attribute does not float free. Brittle and elastic in the same respect at once is a contradiction, so it is not a pair of attributes the nature contains. The error is either detaching the attribute or loading the nature with a clash. A real attribute is a way the glass is.

exercises.prompt: A student says the glass is fully brittle and fully elastic in the same blow, in the same respect, and that both constitute its nature. What is the clash?

choices.text: An error in the description, not a richer nature
A permissible feature of specific attributes
Elasticity as man-made and brittleness as given, so both may be kept
The blow, which functions as a vote

feedback.note: The two attributes contradict in the same respect at the same time, so the clash is an error in thinking, because a specific nature is not a permission to be both. Keeping both does not enrich the nature. The man-made and the given are a different distinction and do not license a contradiction in the glass. The blow is an action, not a vote that constitutes attributes.

exercises.prompt: Someone says the attributes are only our measurements, so the glass has none of its own. What is the error?

choices.text: Measurement identifies attributes the glass has; it does not replace them
Attributes are whatever the measurer wishes
A glass with no attributes is still a specific entity
Measurement is constant conjunction and therefore the attribute

feedback.note: The glass has its attributes, and measurement apprehends them, because identification is not creation. A wish does not constitute brittleness. A glass with no attributes is not a specific entity. Constant conjunction is a theory of causal sequence, not an account of what an attribute is. The error is moving the attributes out of the entity and into the measurer, which is primacy of consciousness.

exercises.prompt: Complete the statement of what a nature is made of.

parts.text: A nature is made of specific

feedback.note: A nature is made of specific attributes, because that is what it is for an entity to be something rather than a bare particular. Wishes and votes would make the nature a mental product. A void has no attributes to contribute. The glass is transparent, brittle, and solid as the glass, not as a list someone's preference assembled.

exercises.prompt: Assemble the relation of attributes to the nature.

feedback.note: Specific attributes make up the entity's nature, because they are not extras and not substitutes for the entity. "Wishes" would move them into consciousness. "Replace" is what a floating attribute tries to do to the entity, and it fails. The pane remains the something. Transparency remains a way it is. Neither is a free-standing existent.

exercises.prompt: What does an entity's action follow from?

choices.text: What that entity is
A demand that ignores its nature
A free-floating attribute
Chance, added beside its nature

feedback.note: Action follows from what the entity is, because causality is identity applied to action and the attributes constitute the nature that acts. A demand that ignores the nature asks for a contradiction. A floating attribute has nothing to act. Chance is not a partner cause. The action is the entity's action, including, for a volitional consciousness, the choice to focus or not.

exercises.prompt: Glass shatters under a sharp blow and does not stretch like rubber. Why?

choices.text: Shattering follows from what the glass is
The blow is a decree and the glass has no nature
Rubber and glass share one nature, so the difference is unreal
The expectation of shattering is the cause

feedback.note: The glass shatters because that action follows from its nature, the attributes that make it brittle rather than elastic. A decree would be a will set over the pane. One shared nature would erase the difference between glass and rubber. Expectation is Humean constant conjunction, placing the cause in the observer. The blow is the action of the striker on an entity of this kind.

exercises.prompt: A coach demands that the pane "act like steel just this once." What is he demanding?

choices.text: That the glass act against its nature
An ordinary change, which identity always permits
A difference that is only a matter of voting
A minor cause the law of identity allows beside the nature

feedback.note: He is demanding an action against the glass's nature, because steel and glass are not the same something and one blow does not make them so. Ordinary change is a later state of the same nature, or a different entity, not a contradiction on demand. A vote does not constitute the pane. There is no minor cause beside the nature. The demand is the longer clause's rejected case.

exercises.prompt: A person chooses to focus. How does "action follows" apply without turning the choice into a flood?

choices.text: The choice follows from the nature of a volitional consciousness; it could have gone the other way
The choice follows from no nature at all
